findings.claim: In stringifySetCookie, the custom `options.encode` function (a documented, callable public option) is never invoked when `cookie.value` is an empty string (or undefined). The code computes `const value = cookie.value ? enc(cookie.value) : "";`, using a truthiness check instead of an undefined check. Since an empty string is falsy, `enc` is silently bypassed for empty-string values and its result is discarded, even though the value is a legitimate, defined string. This is inconsistent with the sibling function stringifyCookie, which always calls `enc(val)` for any defined value (including empty string), and it violates the documented contract that `encode` 'will be used to encode a cookie-value' whenever a value is provided. Any caller relying on a custom encode function to run unconditionally on defined values (e.g., for logging, mandatory prefixing/signing, or side effects) will have that behavior silently skipped for empty-string cookie values.

findings.claim: stringifySetCookie uses a truthiness check (`cookie.value ? enc(cookie.value) : ""`) instead of an undefined check, so when `value` is an empty string the caller-supplied `encode` function from `options.encode` is never invoked. This silently diverges from the documented contract of the `encode` option ("a function that will be used to encode a cookie-value") and from the sibling API `stringifyCookie`, which unconditionally calls `enc(val)` for any defined value (including the empty string) at line 172 (`const value = enc(val);`). Any consumer relying on a custom encode function to run for every provided value (e.g. to sign, hash, or tag the value) will get an unencoded empty string instead, for the specific case of an explicit empty-string cookie value.

findings.claim: stringifySetCookie's path validation (pathValueRegExp) incorrectly rejects the '<' character (U+003C) in the `path` option, even though the function's own documented grammar for path-value is 'any CHAR except CTLs or ";"' (i.e. only control characters and semicolon should be excluded). The regex ranges skip over < entirely, so a syntactically valid path containing '<' (e.g. '/foo<bar') throws a TypeError ('option path is invalid') instead of being serialized, unlike '>' which is correctly allowed by the same regex. This is an asymmetric/off-by-one range bug: the analogous cookieNameRegExp correctly special-cases and includes < as an allowed character, but pathValueRegExp omits it.

findings.claim: stringifySetCookie's maxAge validation only checks Number.isInteger(cookie.maxAge), but a large-magnitude integer (>= 1e21) is still an integer under IEEE-754 semantics while its JavaScript string coercion switches to scientific notation. The resulting 'Max-Age' attribute value (e.g. '1e+21') violates the max-age-value grammar defined by RFC 6265 sec 5.6.2 (which the function's own JSDoc references) and does not match the module's own maxAgeRegExp (/^-?\d+$/) used elsewhere to parse Max-Age. This produces a syntactically malformed Set-Cookie header attribute that passes validation silently instead of being rejected or correctly formatted.

findings.claim: Cache.__setitem__ (inherited unchanged by LRUCache) computes its eviction-loop threshold as `self.__currsize + size > maxsize` instead of `self.__currsize - old_size + size > maxsize` when updating an EXISTING key to a larger size. Because the key's own current (stale) size is never subtracted before the capacity check, the loop overestimates required free space by exactly the old size of the key being updated. This causes the cache to evict other, unrelated entries even when the update would fit within maxsize without any eviction, violating the capacity invariant that eviction should only occur when strictly necessary and needlessly destroying unrelated cached entries (verified reproducible on LRUCache, which delegates directly to this method via `cache_setitem=Cache.__setitem__`).

findings.claim: When updating an existing key's value to a larger sizeof-weighted size, Cache.__setitem__ (inherited by LRUCache) evicts more entries than necessary. The eviction-trigger condition `while self.__currsize + size > maxsize` compares the *new* size against a `self.__currsize` that still includes the key's *old* size (the old size is only subtracted afterward via `diffsize`). This double-counts the key being updated (old size + new size simultaneously) while deciding how many items to evict, causing unrelated entries that would still fit to be evicted from the LRU cache even though the final state would have fit within maxsize without evicting them.

findings.claim: An empty string bypasses the custom encoder. Empty strings are valid public values, and an encoder may legitimately transform them into a nonempty representation. The truthiness check silently discards that transformation, breaking custom encoding schemes.

Max-Age validation accepts integers that serialize in exponential notation, producing an invalid Max-Age attribute. For example, 1e21 passes Number.isInteger but becomes '1e+21', whereas Max-Age requires decimal digits with an optional leading minus. Clients can ignore the malformed lifetime, including a negative lifetime intended to expire a cookie.

The custom encoder is silently skipped for an empty-string value, even though this is a valid string input. Encoders that map empty strings to a nonempty representation therefore produce incorrect cookies.

Large integer maxAge values pass validation but serialize in exponential notation, which is not a valid Max-Age integer representation. In particular, a large negative value intended to expire a cookie can instead generate an ignored attribute.

A custom encoder can mutate cookie.name after its validation but before serialization. The function then emits an unvalidated name, allowing forbidden delimiters into the header despite the name-validation check.

A custom encode callback can mutate cookie.name after validation, causing an unvalidated name to be emitted. Even with string-typed inputs and a string-returning encoder, this permits cookie-value substitution and attribute injection. Capture the name once and serialize that validated value, or validate the final name after invoking the callback.

Max-Age validation accepts integers whose string representation uses scientific notation. Values such as 1e21 and -1e21 produce invalid Max-Age attributes, which cookie clients ignore; the negative case therefore fails to request immediate expiry. Emit decimal integer syntax or reject unsupported magnitudes.

findings.claim: A custom encode callback can bypass cookie-name validation by mutating the input object. The name is validated before invoking encode but read again afterward, allowing an unvalidated name to replace the cookie value and inject attributes. Capture and serialize the validated name, or validate the actual name used after the callback.

Large integer maxAge values pass validation but are emitted in exponential notation, which is not a valid Max-Age integer representation. In particular, a large negative value intended to expire a cookie produces an invalid attribute instead. Reject unsupported magnitudes or serialize them as decimal integers.

Growing an existing value unnecessarily evicts other entries, even when the resulting mapping fits within capacity. Cache.__setitem__ tests current size plus the entire replacement size without crediting the replaced value. This affects both Cache and LRUCache.

A supplied callable getsizeof with false truth value is silently ignored. Both Cache and LRUCache then use unit accounting rather than the configured size function, accepting values exceeding the configured capacity.

Growing an existing value can evict unrelated entries even when the replacement fits within capacity. Cache.__setitem__ tests currsize plus the entire replacement size before subtracting the old value's size. This affects both Cache and LRUCache: a replacement that brings total size from 9 to exactly 10 instead discards another entry and leaves total size 6.

A valid configurable getsizeof callable is silently ignored if it is falsey. The constructor checks truthiness rather than whether the argument is None, so both Cache and LRUCache fall back to unit accounting, retain values whose configured total exceeds maxsize, and accept individually oversized values.

findings.claim: Cache silently ignores a valid false-valued getsizeof callable. Both Cache and LRUCache consequently use unit accounting instead of the configured weights, retaining entries beyond the requested capacity and accepting individually oversized values. The optional callback should be selected by whether it is None, not its truth value.

A NaN result from getsizeof passes size validation and permanently poisons currsize until clear(), disabling capacity enforcement in both Cache and LRUCache. Even deleting the offending entry leaves NaN accounting, so subsequent ordinary unit-sized entries accumulate without eviction. NaN must be rejected before mutation because it is not a valid non-negative size.

items: Expose explicit source line numbers and validate citation bindings before terminal delivery.

postTrialFollowup.measurementBoundary: Later gateway, harness or prompt fixes require a new declaration and fresh trials. This report records the original b91aa88 protocol and does not attribute later fixes to its outcomes.

lifecycleResearch.interpretation: Separate synthetic experiments reproduced shutdown interruption during delayed final hashing and a modern discovery audit-reservation conflict. These are demonstrated possible mechanisms, not proof of the cause of any missing end in the historical trial. Later boundary verification does not repair the frozen trial.

limits: Two purposively selected historical defect families, four snapshots and one observation per cell; no unseen holdout, model ranking or MCP effectiveness claim.

Source and test packets are curated selections, not full upstream CI. The alpha.5 cookie trial uses an explicitly locked Vitest5 tooling override; original Vitest4 incompatibility is retained separately.
Capability restrictions are client-version-specific. Authenticated client processes are outside the execution containers; local orchestration is not local model inference.
Original citation errors, missing calls, lifecycle gaps and budget overruns remain protocol failures even when judges confirm the observed behavior.
Both judge attempts are protocol-incomplete. Core execution support and score agreement do not repair their omissions or establish normative API correctness.
MCP native validation coverage and semantic API defect discovery are different outcomes.
Provider token accounting and medium effort settings do not establish equivalent compute budgets. Subscription billing remains unknown.
